title: MGRS Converter: Military Grid Reference System
description: Convert between coordinates and MGRS references with the MGRS Converter — grid zones, 100 km squares and digit precision explained. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, Times Square's MGRS reference is 18T WL 85632 12388 at metre precision — a single string that finds a doorway, spoken by soldiers, rescuers and surveyors worldwide.

body.t: MGRS is the lingua franca of joint operations and much field science — convert a GPS pair to a reference that can be spoken, written and plotted identically by everyone.
Reports cite MGRS. The converter turns their strings back into map points — pair with the
The digits' precision ladder (2 digits = 10 km … 10 digits = 1 m) is the curriculum — this page computes references to practise against.
Field projects in many regions log finds by MGRS; the converter bridges those logs and GIS.

18T: grid zone (UTM zone 18, latitude band T). WL: the 100 km square. 85632 / 12388: easting and northing within the square at metre precision (from UTM E 585,633, N 4,512,388). Drop digit pairs and the reference coarsens gracefully — 18T WL 85 12 is the 1 km version.

Even digit totals split half/half between easting and northing: 4 digits → 1 km squares, 6 → 100 m, 8 → 10 m, 10 → 1 m. The reference contains its own uncertainty statement, which is why professionals trust the format.

popular_table.title: MGRS structure
rows: UTM zone number + latitude band letter (C–X, no I/O)
Two letters from the UTM lettering scheme
Easting then northing within the square, truncated (never rounded)
Digit pairs: 2→10 km, 4→1 km, 6→100 m, 8→10 m, 10→1 m
popular_table.note: Polar regions switch to UPS (letters A/B/Y/Z zones) — the converter handles the standard's both halves. Truncation (not rounding) is specified so a reference always names the square containing the point.

faq: What does this tool calculate?
The MGRS reference for coordinates (UTM/UPS-based, with 100 km square letters and digits), and the coordinates for a reference — the NATO grid standard (MIL-STD-60007 family) as published.
Do I need an account?
No — and no callsign, unit or permission; the system is a public standard.
Can I use the result for professional work?

MGRS is a working professional standard in defence, emergency and field-science contexts, and this converter implements its published lettering and truncation rules. Operational use follows your organisation's own validated tools, as with any standard.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84 — tile systems are defined over it.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
No — tiles and pixels quantise; decimals beyond the cell are decoration.
Can I copy the result into GIS software?
As a label directly; as geometry via the converted coordinates — most defence-adjacent GIS speaks MGRS natively.
Letters I and O missing — why?
Excluded from bands and squares to prevent confusion with 1 and 0 — the same human-factors courtesy as the British grid's missing I.
Truncated, not rounded?
Always truncated: 85632 could be anything from 85632.0 to 85632.9 — the reference claims the square, not the point, and truncation keeps the claim true.
Datum warnings?
MGRS rides WGS84 in its modern form; references derived from old local datums can sit hundreds of metres off. Documents should state their datum; converters assume WGS84.
UPS polar zones?
Above 84°N and below 80°S, UTM yields to UPS with its own lettering — the converter switches systems at the standard's boundary.
Square letters repeat?
Every ~2,000 km the lettering cycles — the grid zone designator disambiguates, which is why full references always carry it.
GARS instead?
Area referencing (30′ cells) versus MGRS's point precision — the GARS Converter covers the area system; choose by the conversation you are joining.
